actions.title: Local Enumeration Sweep
actions.hypothesis: Privesc is won by enumeration, not memory. Run a scanner (linpeas) for breadth, but read it with intent: you are looking for the ONE anomaly — a weird SUID, a writable path, a credential in a config — not reading the whole rainbow. Then verify manually before burning time on an exploit.
actions.proves: establishes local privilege escalation leads, host kernel/version, host architecture
actions.does_not_prove: local privilege escalation lead only — not admin/root/SYSTEM until separately proven

commands.note: Serve from your box (mentor can host it). Pipe to tee to keep a local copy as evidence.
The holy trinity: what can I sudo, who am I, who else exists.
SUID, capabilities, cron — the three most common lab wins in one line.

actions.title: sudo / GTFOBins Abuse
actions.hypothesis: sudo -l entries on common binaries are usually instant root: anything GTFOBins lists with a sudo section (vim, find, awk, tar, less, python...) has a documented shell escape. NOPASSWD entries are the gift-wrap.
actions.does_not_prove: root/admin only when command output proves it; discovered local leads alone are not privileged access

commands.note: Read every entry. Cross-reference each binary against gtfobins.github.io.
Generic pattern; the exact escape depends on the binary — GTFOBins gives the precise command per tool.

actions.title: Writable /etc/passwd
actions.hypothesis: If /etc/passwd is world-writable (it happens in labs more than you would think), you can append a new root-equivalent user with a password hash you generate locally. No exploit needed — the file IS the security boundary, and it is open.
actions.does_not_prove: root/admin only when command output proves it; discovered local leads alone are not privileged access

commands.note: Confirm the write bit. -rw-rw-rw- means go.
Generate the hash LOCALLY first.
Append the forged user, then: su r00t. Replace HASH_FROM_OPENSSL with your generated hash.

actions.title: NFS no_root_squash
actions.hypothesis: An NFS export with no_root_squash trusts remote root: mount it from your attacking position (or from a foothold), drop a SUID binary or a root-owned shell, and execute it as root on the target.
actions.does_not_prove: root/admin only when command output proves it; discovered local leads alone are not privileged access

commands.note: List exports; look for no_root_squash in /etc/exports on the foothold if you cannot see options directly.
Plant a SUID bash on the share...
...then run it on the target with -p to keep effective-root.

actions.title: LXC/LXD Group Escape
actions.hypothesis: Membership in the lxd group is passwordless root: lxd lets you create a privileged container, mount the host filesystem into it, and read/write anything as root. This is one of the most common intended privesc paths in HTB/0xdf boxes. If `id` shows lxd (or lxc), the box is already beaten — the rest is ceremony.
actions.does_not_prove: root/admin only when command output proves it; discovered local leads alone are not privileged access

commands.note: Confirm lxd or lxc group membership before anything else.
If an image already exists, use it. If not, build one locally: clone lxc-alpine-builder, build alpine.tar.gz, transfer it, then `lxc image import alpine.tar.gz --alias alpine`.
Privileged container = container root is host root.

commands.run: lxc config device add privesc host-root disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true
commands.note: Mount the entire host filesystem into the container.

commands.run: lxc start privesc && lxc exec privesc /bin/sh
commands.note: Inside the container, /mnt/root is the host filesystem as root. Read flags, add users, done.

actions.title: Docker Socket / docker Group Escape
actions.hypothesis: A writable /var/run/docker.sock (or docker group membership) is equivalent to root on the host: run a container with the host filesystem mounted and chroot in. Same logic as LXD, different daemon.
actions.does_not_prove: root/admin only when command output proves it; discovered local leads alone are not privileged access

commands.note: Socket writable by you, or docker group membership → game over.
Pick any existing image to avoid network pulls.
Host filesystem at /mnt, as root. Substitute an image from docker images output.

actions.title: SUID Binary Abuse
actions.hypothesis: SUID binaries run as their owner (usually root). The system ones (su, sudo, mount) are fine — you are hunting the ANOMALY: a custom or unexpected binary with the SUID bit. Cross-reference anything unusual against GTFOBins; the corpus is full of boxes where find / -perm -4000 is the entire privesc.
actions.proves: establishes administrative/root access, local privilege escalation leads
actions.does_not_prove: root/admin only when command output proves it; discovered local leads alone are not privileged access

commands.note: List all SUID binaries. Compare against the default set — anything non-standard is your lead.
SUID + SGID with ownership details. SGID on interesting groups (adm → read /var/log, shadow → crack root).

actions.title: Process Monitoring (pspy)
actions.hypothesis: Cron jobs and timers run commands as root that you cannot see in /etc/crontab. pspy watches process creation WITHOUT root and reveals them: scripts with writable paths, commands leaking credentials in arguments, backup jobs you can hijack. When static enumeration stalls, watching the box breathe is the move — 0xdf reaches for pspy constantly.
actions.proves: establishes process-monitoring privesc lead, candidate credentials
actions.does_not_prove: local privilege escalation lead only — not admin/root/SYSTEM until separately proven

commands.note: Serve pspy from your box (python3 -m http.server), wget it to /tmp or /dev/shm, chmod +x, run. -p shows processes, -f filesystem events, -i poll interval ms.
Poor-man's pspy for short-window jobs. Root processes flashing by = scheduled task.

actions.title: Cron Job Abuse and Tar Wildcards
actions.hypothesis: Two flavors: (1) a root cron job runs a script you can WRITE — edit it, wait, root. (2) A root job runs tar/rsync/chown with a WILDCARD in a directory you control — you cannot edit the command, but you can plant files whose NAMES inject options (tartarsauce: --checkpoint-action=exec). Wildcard injection is the trick nobody sees coming.
actions.does_not_prove: root/admin only when command output proves it; discovered local leads alone are not privileged access

report.finding: Cron Job Abuse Leading to Root

commands.note: Enumerate jobs. For each script: can you write it? Is its directory writable? Does it use wildcards?
Writable root-run script: append a SUID dropper, wait for the cycle, run /tmp/rootbash -p.

commands.run: cd /writable/backup/dir && touch -- '--checkpoint=1' '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh shell.sh' && echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/b; chmod +s /tmp/b' > shell.sh
commands.note: Tar wildcard injection: filenames that ARE options. When root's tar -cf ... * runs, your checkpoint executes. Same trick works for rsync (--rsh) and chown (--reference).

actions.title: Linux Capabilities Abuse
actions.hypothesis: Capabilities split root's powers — and misassigned ones are privesc: cap_setuid on python/perl = instant root shell, cap_dac_read_search = read any file (shadow), cap_sys_admin ≈ root. getcap finds them; GTFOBins has a capabilities section for each interpreter.
actions.does_not_prove: root/admin only when command output proves it; discovered local leads alone are not privileged access

commands.note: List all file capabilities. Anything on an interpreter (python, perl, ruby, php, openssl, tcpdump) is a lead.
cap_setuid on python → root shell. Perl: perl -e 'use POSIX qw(setuid); POSIX::setuid(0); exec "/bin/sh";'
cap_net_raw on tcpdump → sniff the wire from the foothold; creds in cleartext protocols land in your lap.

actions.title: Loot Hunting (Linux)
actions.hypothesis: Before exotic privesc, hunt loot: history files, config files with passwords, other users' readable home dirs, /opt and /var backups, mail spools. The corpus turns up credentials in history files and configs constantly — and .bash_history symlinked to /dev/null is itself a hint that the author hid something elsewhere.
actions.does_not_prove: credential material only — not access until it authenticates against a service

commands.note: History files: commands leak passwords passed as arguments, paths, other hosts.
Config grep sweep. /var/www configs hold DB creds; /opt holds backup scripts with embedded passwords.
Mail spools (beep pattern), temp dirs, backups, key material, KeePass vaults.

actions.title: Linux Persistence (Post-Root)
actions.hypothesis: After root, leave a door that survives password resets and reboots — useful in long labs and when the exam lets you return. The quiet options: your SSH key in root's authorized_keys, a sudoers line for a low-priv user you control, or a cron callback. (Report everything you plant.)
actions.does_not_prove: persistence setup context — document and clean up; not a new privilege level

commands.note: The corpus standard (admirer, brainfuck, armageddon). Generate the keypair on YOUR box first: ssh-keygen -t ed25519.
Sudoers backdoor for a user you already control — survives root password changes.
Cron callback. Noisier; prefer keys when SSH is exposed.
